title: Find Peak Element
directAnswer: Return the index of *any* peak — an element strictly greater than both neighbors — where out-of-bounds neighbors count as −∞. The surprise is that you can do this in O(log n) on an UNSORTED array: compare nums[mid] with nums[mid+1] and always walk uphill. If nums[mid] < nums[mid+1] a peak must exist to the right, so go right; otherwise a peak exists at mid or to the left. Use `while (lo < hi)` with `hi = mid` (not mid − 1) and return `lo`.

remember.pattern: Binary search on a slope — always climb toward the higher neighbor
rules: Binary search works even though the array is **unsorted** — the monotonicity is in the *slope*, not the values.
Compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[mid + 1]`; `mid` is computed by floor division so `mid + 1` is always in bounds while `lo < hi`.
Use `while (lo < hi)` with `hi = mid` — **not** `mid - 1` — because `mid` itself could be the peak and must stay in the window.
Treat `nums[-1] = nums[n] = -∞`. The boundaries are the lowest, so a peak is guaranteed to exist and the search never falls off the ends.
The window always contains a peak (the **invariant**); when it shrinks to one element, that element is a peak — return `lo`.
whenToUse: Find a local maximum / any peak where neighbors are defined and ends are −∞
The array isn't sorted but adjacent comparisons give a *direction* to move
You only need *one* valid answer, not all peaks
'Walk uphill' / 'gradient' style reasoning over an index range
antiSignals: You need *all* peaks → a single linear scan is required, O(n)
Neighbors aren't comparable or there's no notion of 'uphill' → binary search has no direction to follow
The 'peak' is a global max with ties that matter → this finds *a* local peak, not a specific one
remember.takeaway: Find Peak Element shatters the myth that binary search needs a sorted array. What it really needs is a *monotone decision* — here, 'is the slope going up?' — that lets one comparison discard half the indices. Master this and you'll spot binary search in rotated arrays, Koko Eating Bananas, and any 'follow the gradient' problem.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realise binary search applies to an UNSORTED array because the *slope* is what's exploited, and whether you can argue the correctness invariant ('a peak always lives inside [lo, hi]') rather than just pattern-matching to a template.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Assuming binary search needs sorted input and defaulting to an O(n) scan, or writing `hi = mid - 1` (which can throw away the only peak) and `while (lo <= hi)` (which over-runs and reads out of bounds).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Prove the invariant: if `nums[mid] < nums[mid+1]`, the right side starts by rising and ends at −∞, so it MUST turn around at some peak — therefore a peak is guaranteed on the right. Then explain why `hi = mid` keeps that peak in the window.

problemStatement:
A peak element is an element that is **strictly greater** than its neighbors.

Given a 0-indexed integer array `nums`, find a peak element, and return its index. If the array contains multiple peaks, return the index to **any** of the peaks.

You may imagine that `nums[-1] = nums[n] = -∞`. In other words, an element is always considered to be strictly greater than a neighbor that is outside the array.

You must write an algorithm that runs in `O(log n)` time.
constraints: nums[i] != nums[i + 1] for all valid i (no two adjacent values are equal)
understanding: We want any index that is a local maximum, with imaginary −∞ sentinels beyond both ends. Because the ends are −∞ and no two adjacent values are equal, a peak always exists. The non-obvious part: even though `nums` is not sorted, the *direction of the slope* at any midpoint tells us which half is guaranteed to still contain a peak, so we can halve the search space in O(log n).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the array values sorted in any way?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — and that's the interesting part. We don't need sortedness; we need that adjacent elements differ, which gives every midpoint a clear uphill or downhill direction.

clarifyingQuestions.question: If there are several peaks, which one do I return?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Any of them. The problem explicitly accepts any valid peak index, which is exactly why binary search is allowed to commit to one half.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about the boundaries — can index 0 or n−1 be a peak?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. With `nums[-1] = nums[n] = -∞`, a strictly increasing array peaks at the last index, and a strictly decreasing one peaks at index 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can adjacent elements be equal?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — the constraint guarantees `nums[i] != nums[i+1]`. That's essential: equal neighbors would create flat regions with no slope to follow.

approaches.name: Linear Scan (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: State it as the obvious O(n) baseline, then surprise the interviewer by claiming O(log n) is possible despite the array being unsorted.
hints: Forget cleverness: walk left to right. When does an element stop being smaller than the next one?
Return the first index `i` where `nums[i] > nums[i + 1]` — that's a peak, because everything before kept rising to it.
If you never find such a descent, the array is strictly increasing, so the last index is the peak.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass over up to n − 1 adjacent comparisons, no extra memory.
approaches.explanation:
Scan from the front comparing each element to its right neighbor. Return the first index `i` with `nums[i] > nums[i + 1]`. If no such index exists, the array rose all the way to the end, so return `n - 1`.

**Why the first descent is a peak.** Reading left to right, the moment the sequence stops increasing (`nums[i] > nums[i + 1]`) we know `nums[i]` is greater than its right neighbor. It's also greater than its left neighbor: either `i == 0` (left neighbor is −∞) or we only reached `i` because `nums[i - 1] < nums[i]` (otherwise the descent would have triggered earlier). Both neighbors are smaller, so `nums[i]` is a peak.

**Why mention it.** It's a correct, easy-to-justify baseline that establishes the O(n) cost we're about to beat. Saying 'the naive scan is O(n)' frames the improvement and shows you can reason about *why* an element qualifies as a peak — the same reasoning the binary search will lean on.

**Why it's not the intended answer.** The prompt demands `O(log n)`. The scan inspects potentially every element, ignoring that a single comparison at the midpoint already tells us which half must contain a peak. That directional information is exactly what lets us discard half the array at a time.
approaches.insight: The scan only learns 'is this the first descent?' one element at a time. Binary search reuses the *same* descent reasoning — but applied at the midpoint, where one comparison rules out an entire half because the −∞ boundary guarantees the kept half still turns around somewhere.

java.explanation: First descent: nums[i] beats its right neighbor, and (by how we got here) its left neighbor too.
Never descended → strictly increasing → the last element is the peak (right neighbor is −∞).

python.explanation: First index greater than its right neighbor is guaranteed to be a peak.
Strictly increasing array peaks at the final index.

pitfalls: Looping `i` to `nums.length` instead of `nums.length - 1` — reads `nums[i + 1]` out of bounds.
Forgetting the trailing `return n - 1` for a strictly increasing array.
Shipping this when the prompt asks for O(log n).

approaches.name: Binary Search Uphill (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Lead with the counter-intuitive claim — 'binary search on an unsorted array' — and back it with the −∞-boundary guarantee.
hints: You can't sort, but you can ask a directional question at the middle: is the slope at `mid` going up or down?
Compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[mid + 1]`. If it's rising, a peak must lie to the right (the right end is −∞, so it has to turn around). If it's falling, a peak lies at `mid` or to the left.
Keep the window with `while (lo < hi)` and set `lo = mid + 1` when rising, `hi = mid` when falling. The window always holds a peak; return `lo`.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each iteration discards half the window, so it runs in ⌈log₂ n⌉ = O(log n) steps. Only scalar variables are used → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain a window `[lo, hi]` that **always contains at least one peak**. Initialise `lo = 0`, `hi = n - 1`. While `lo < hi`, compute `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` and compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[mid + 1]`. If `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]` we're on an upward slope, so move `lo = mid + 1`. Otherwise we're on a downward (or flat-impossible) slope, so move `hi = mid`. When `lo == hi` the window is a single index — that element is a peak — return `lo`.

**Why a peak is guaranteed in the kept half.** Suppose `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]` (rising). Look at the subarray from `mid + 1` to `n - 1`. It *starts* by going up (since `nums[mid+1] > nums[mid]`) and it *ends* at the −∞ sentinel beyond index `n - 1`. A sequence that rises and then must fall to −∞ has to turn around somewhere — that turning point is a peak. So discarding indices `0..mid` is safe: a peak still exists in `[mid + 1, hi]`. The mirror argument holds when `nums[mid] > nums[mid + 1]`: the left part `[lo, mid]` ends high at `mid` and is bounded by −∞ on the far left, so it contains a peak — and `mid` itself might be it, which is why we keep `mid`.

**Why `hi = mid` and never `mid - 1`.** When the slope falls at `mid`, `mid` is a *candidate peak* — it beats its right neighbor and might beat its left one too. Writing `hi = mid - 1` would evict `mid` from the window and could throw away the only peak (e.g. `nums = [3, 2, 1]`, where index 0 is the answer). Keeping `hi = mid` preserves the invariant 'the window contains a peak'. This is the structural difference from value-search binary search, where you *have* tested `mid` and can safely exclude it.

**Why `while (lo < hi)` and not `<=`.** This template converges the window down to a single surviving index rather than searching for a known value. With `hi = mid`, the condition must be strict `<`: if it were `<=`, then when `lo == hi == mid` we'd evaluate `nums[mid + 1]` — potentially out of bounds at the right edge — and the window would never shrink, looping forever. The strict `<` stops exactly when one element remains.

**Why `mid + 1` is always safe to read.** `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` uses floor division, so whenever `lo < hi` we have `mid < hi <= n - 1`, hence `mid + 1 <= n - 1` is a valid index. The loop guard and the floor together guarantee we never read past the end.

**Why termination is guaranteed.** Every branch strictly shrinks the window: `lo = mid + 1` raises the lower bound past `mid`, and `hi = mid` lowers the upper bound below its old value (because `mid < hi`). A strictly shrinking non-empty integer window must reach `lo == hi`.
approaches.insight: Binary search doesn't require sorted *values* — it requires a *monotone decision* that lets one probe eliminate half the candidates. Here the decision is 'which way is uphill?', and the −∞ boundaries guarantee the uphill direction always leads to a peak. Reframing 'sorted' as 'has a halving decision' is the unlock for rotated-array search, 'binary search on the answer', and every gradient-style problem.

pitfalls: Writing `hi = mid - 1` — can discard the only peak (e.g. [3,2,1] would miss index 0).
Using `while (lo <= hi)` with `hi = mid` — reads nums[mid + 1] out of bounds and never terminates.
Comparing `nums[mid]` with `nums[mid - 1]` instead of `nums[mid + 1]` — the template no longer matches the bound updates.
Assuming binary search is illegal because the array isn't sorted — the slope provides the needed monotone decision.

commonMistakes: Believing binary search requires sorted input and defaulting to an O(n) scan.
Using `hi = mid - 1` instead of `hi = mid`, which can evict the only peak from the window.
Pairing `hi = mid` with `while (lo <= hi)` — causes an out-of-bounds read and an infinite loop.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Excluding mid when going left
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On a downward slope, `mid` is itself a peak candidate. `hi = mid - 1` removes it; for [3, 2, 1] the only peak is index 0 and this throws it away, returning a wrong index or running out of bounds.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if (nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]) lo = mid + 1;
else hi = mid - 1;
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if (nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]) lo = mid + 1;
else hi = mid;

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong loop condition for the hi = mid template
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With `hi = mid`, the window can stall at `lo == hi`. Using `<=` keeps the loop alive there, evaluates `nums[mid + 1]` at the right edge (out of bounds), and never terminates. Strict `<` stops with one element.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Overflow in the midpoint
commonMistakesDetailed.why: In Java `lo + hi` is a 32-bit int and can overflow for large indices, wrapping negative. Use the difference form even when the array is small — it's a free habit.

patternNote: Binary search driven by a *slope* rather than sorted values. Recognise it whenever an adjacent comparison gives a guaranteed direction toward the answer and any single valid result is acceptable. The defining moves are `hi = mid` (keep the candidate) with `while (lo < hi)`; the same skeleton solves Peak Index in a Mountain Array and the 2D peak problem.
